user.description: JFL panels dial out to Home Assistant, so this integration listens and waits. Choose the TCP port to listen on; it must match the reporting destination programmed into the panel. Everything else — model, partitions, zones and the electric fence — is detected from the panel itself.

panel_never_connected.description:
Nothing has reported to {host}:{port} in {minutes} minutes.

JFL panels dial out to Home Assistant rather than the other way round, so the panel has to be programmed to report here:

1. In the panel's programming, set a **free** reporting destination IP to this machine's address and the port above. Do not overwrite the slot your monitoring company uses.
2. Enable dual reporting at address 700, TECLA8, so the existing monitoring connection keeps working.
3. Check the permissions at address 300.

If the panel is on a different network, make sure this port is reachable from it.
panel_never_connected.title: No JFL panel has connected

remote_access_blocked.description:
Panel {serial} answered a command with "wrong password", and this integration has stopped sending anything that carries one.

**Five wrong passwords block remote operation at the panel** until somebody performs a valid operation on the keypad, so no further attempt will be made automatically.

This should not be possible: none of the commands this integration sends carries a password. Please report it with a diagnostics download — it means a genuine bug, and the frames in that download are what will identify it.
remote_access_blocked.title: Panel rejected a password

unknown_model.description:
Panel {serial} reports model byte {model_byte}, which is not in this integration's model table.

The integration has assumed a permissive set of capabilities so that entities still appear, which may mean partitions or zones that do not really exist. Please report the model byte and the panel's commercial name so it can be added.
unknown_model.title: Unrecognised panel model

unsupported_model.description:
Panel {serial} reports as a {model} ({model_byte}). This integration implements that model from JFL's specification, but nobody has verified it against real hardware — only the Active 32 Duo has been.

Everything should work. If something does not, please report it: the model byte and a diagnostics download are exactly what is needed to fix it.
unsupported_model.title: Panel model not tested

data.unknown_panels: Panels that are not configured yet

data_description.keepalive_minutes: How often the panel is told to check in. A panel that says nothing for two and a half times this long is treated as gone.
data_description.log_raw_frames: Adds the bytes of every frame to the debug log. Only useful when investigating a decoding problem, and it only appears if debug logging is enabled for this integration.
data_description.programming_read_interval: How often to re-read the panel's programming, which is where zone and partition names live. A panel is always read once automatically when it first connects, so names appear without pressing anything; this only controls the repeat. Set to 0 to read once and never again. A re-read costs nothing when the programming has not changed — the panel publishes a checksum that says so.
data_description.unknown_panels: What to do when a panel reports in that has not been added yet.

init.description: These settings apply to the listener and to every panel that reports to it.
init.title: JFL Alarm options

read_event_buffer.description: Returns the panel's own event memory — every arm, disarm, alarm, bypass and trouble it recorded, including while Home Assistant was off. It only reads, so it works in read-only mode. These events are returned as data and are deliberately NOT replayed onto the event entities: replaying a stored panic would run every automation listening for one.

limit.description: How many records to return at most. The panel pages eight at a time, so a large limit is a long conversation on a link that is also polling the status.
limit.name: Maximum events

since_serial.description: The event serial to page forward from. The buffer is read oldest first and there is no way to ask for the newest, so keep the 'next_serial' a call returns and pass it back here to read only what is new. 0 starts at the oldest record the panel still holds.
since_serial.name: Resume from serial

read_event_buffer.name: Read the panel's event buffer

read_programming.description: Reads the panel's programming and returns it — the zone and partition names above all, which is where they live. It takes a few seconds: the panel is asked in paced blocks so the read does not starve the status poll or the keypad. It only reads, so it works in read-only mode, and it never returns a user's access code.
read_programming.name: Read the panel's programming

refresh_status.description: Asks the panel for a status frame now. The panel reports its state only when asked, so this is how you get an immediate update. It reads and never changes anything, so it works in read-only mode.
refresh_status.name: Refresh status

set_bypass_mask.description: Replaces the panel's manual bypass list with exactly the zones given, in one command. The per-zone bypass switches are the ordinary way in; this exists for clearing every bypass at once, which an empty list does.

zones.description: Every zone that should be inhibited afterwards. Zones not listed are brought back into the alarm. An empty list clears all bypasses.
zones.name: Zones to bypass

set_bypass_mask.name: Set the whole bypass list

sync_time.description: Sets the panel's clock to Home Assistant's local time. Worth doing occasionally: the panel timestamps every event it reports from its own clock, so a panel that has drifted files today's alarm under yesterday.

device_id.description: Which panel to set. A partition sub-device resolves to the panel it is on.
device_id.name: Panel

sync_time.name: Set the panel clock
